app.lead: Records of NASA's two satellite systems (MODIS and VIIRS) were merged into one consistent series. This is not a fire-risk map; it shows past fire activity.
info.title: Data and method
info.body: Every number is computed from data by scripts. Labels: measured (counts), estimated (satellite-difference-corrected series, uncertainty band), unverified (claims without an independent reference). See the accuracy report for definitions.

tour.s1: Hi, I'm Lintu! We merged 26 years of Turkey fire records from NASA's two satellite systems (MODIS and VIIRS). Let me show you around the app in one minute.
tour.s2: This is a summary of our work: we cleaned 1.4 million raw satellite detections, counted each fire as a single event, and corrected the false jump caused by the satellite change. Click the boxes to go to the matching screen.
tour.s3: These cards summarise the region and dates you chose: total events, busiest months, the last month against normal, and the 2012 correction.
tour.s4: Scientific mode: when on, the satellite-difference-corrected (MODIS-equivalent) series is shown; click to switch to the raw series. For comparisons across years, scientific mode is the right choice.
tour.s5: Here you choose a province or region and a date range. Every screen updates to match this selection.
tour.s6: Calendar: each row is a year, each column a month. Light colour = many fires. ★ = the busiest months of the year.
tour.s7: On the map, choose the fire type: turn stubble (field burning) on or off.
tour.s8: Click a province on the map to select it. You can also draw a circle or polygon to select your own area.
tour.s9: The events with the highest FRP are listed here. Click one and the map flies there, with its details shown below. The default measure is peak FRP (MW); number one is the 2021 Antalya (Manavgat) event!
tour.s10: Here you see why the raw count jumped artificially when the new satellite was added in 2012, and how we corrected it. Below, one fire is merged step by step.
tour.s11: You can download the tables and charts from here. Simple mode hides technical details for jury presentations, and the EN button switches the language. Happy exploring!

jm.title: What happened in 2012? Same map, three stages
jm.d1: Every satellite point is counted separately. When the new satellite (VIIRS) arrives in 2012 the count jumps artificially: fires did not increase, our eyes got sharper.
jm.d2: Points of the same fire count as one event, and since both satellites are clustered together, a fire seen by both is still one event. Most of the jump disappears, but not all: VIIRS also sees small fires, so the event count still rises somewhat.
jm.d3: VIIRS counts are converted to the old satellite's (MODIS) scale. The map shows what the old satellite saw; the total comes from the corrected series. The jump is gone and the trend follows the old satellite's own measurement.
jm.change: 2012–14 average vs 2009–11 average: raw {a}% · clustering {b}% · corrected {c}% (old satellite actual {d}%). Clustering both satellites together also prevents double counting; clustering them separately and adding up would give {e}%.
jm.legend: Colour scale is the same for every year: 0 → {mx} (per province)
jm.chart: Index: 2009–11 average = 100. Grey dashed raw, orange merged events, green corrected.
tour.s6b: Click a month in the calendar to see its number of events and its five events with the highest peak FRP. Click a year to see its busiest month. In the day grid you can pick a single day too.
tour.s9b: 2012 jump mode: see the same map in three stages. Raw detections jump artificially, clustering removes most of the jump, and the correction removes the rest.
tour.s10b: The science is here: physics, formulas, validation and a comparison with real fires. There I'll take you on a separate science tour.
rep.label: Exclude recurring burns (sensitivity)
rep.help: Events in a ~1 km cell that burned in 3 or more different years are suspected field/stubble burning; forest fires do not recur at the same place every year. Official figures apply with this box unchecked. None of the 19 documented real forest fires is caught by this filter.
rep.note: {n} events ({p}%) removed as suspected recurring burns in this filter.
tour.a1: Hi, I'm Lintu! This app merges 26 years of Turkey fire records from two NASA satellites (MODIS and VIIRS) into one calendar. The summary cards stay visible behind me; press 'Next' and we will go through everything.
tour.a2: This strip summarises our work in 4 steps: clean raw detections, count one hot-spot cluster as one event, translate both satellites into one language. It matters because comparing raw counts directly would mislead you.
tour.a3: The four cards show total fire events, the busiest month, how the latest month compares with normal, and the 2012 jump correction for your region and dates. They update instantly when you change the filters.
tour.a4: With science mode on you see the satellite-bias-corrected (MODIS-equivalent) series; turn it off for raw counts. Leave it on for fair year-to-year comparison, and toggle it once to see the difference.
tour.a5: Pick a province or region and a date range here; the calendar, map and charts all follow this choice. Try picking a province such as Antalya and watch the results change.
tour.a6: In the calendar each row is a year and each column a month; darker means more events. ★ marks the year's month with the most events and 🔥 the month of its event with the highest peak FRP (highest single detection, MW). Click a month and its events open on the map.
tour.a6b: Clicking a month opens the map with that month's events and lists those with the highest peak FRP; back on the calendar, that month's detail panel (count, top 5 events by peak FRP, provinces) is ready here. ★ and 🔥 cells are a good place to start.
tour.a7: Choose which fire type the map shows: all, excluding stubble, or stubble only (field burning). Turning stubble off makes the other fires clearer.
tour.a8: Click a province to select it, or draw a circle or polygon for your own area. The MODIS–VIIRS comparison map next to the main map shows the same area from each satellite side by side.
tour.a9: Events with the highest FRP are ranked here (default: peak FRP, MW). Click one: the map flies there and its details appear below. Look at number one, the 2021 Antalya (Manavgat) event!
tour.a9b: Jump mode shows the same map in three stages: raw detections spike falsely, clustering removes most of it, correction removes the rest. Use the play button to watch it year by year.
tour.a10: When the new satellite (VIIRS) arrived in 2012 the raw count jumped falsely. This chart overlays the raw, clustered and corrected series; the corrected line removes the jump.
tour.a10b: This is the scientific explanation: physics, formulas, validation. The Simple/Expert toggle at the top simplifies the wording or goes into detail. Start the 'Science tour with Lintu' when you are ready.
tour.a11: Download tables and charts here. Simple mode hides details for the jury presentation and the EN button switches language. Happy exploring!

cal.mk_legend_day: ★ = day with the most events this year · 🔥 = day of the year's event with the highest peak FRP (highest single detection, MW)
cal.tomap_hint: Clicking a month sets the date filter to that month and opens the Map tab; that month's biggest fires appear in the list beside the map. Back on the calendar, the month detail panel is ready too.

jump.how: Grey dashed line (square) = RAW detections: sum of both satellite systems, falsely jumps when the new satellite is added in 2012. Orange line (triangle) = merged event count AFTER cleaning and clustering; its unit is 'events', so it is not directly comparable to detections. Thick green line (circle) = the FINAL output of our processing: VIIRS converted to the MODIS scale (corrected series). Pink dotted line (diamond) = the old satellite's actual value, a control reference.
jump.use: For multi-year trends use the GREEN corrected (MODIS-equivalent) series. The grey raw series and orange event count only show the jump. For province comparisons use measured event counts; the province-level equivalent series is not validated.
pix.how: Each bar is the number of RAW satellite detections with that pixel size (no cleaning or correction applied). Pink = MODIS, yellow = VIIRS. Pixels grow towards the scan edge; dotted lines mark nadir (p05) and edge (p95).
pix.use: Use this real size distribution when judging area or location precision; do not assume a fixed 1 km (MODIS) or 375 m (VIIRS).

mc.title: MODIS–VIIRS merging
mc.intro: The real raw points of the event you picked on the main map. Step through.
mc.aria: Small map of the selected event's MODIS and VIIRS points
mc.i0: Click an event on the main map or use 'Go to the event with the highest peak FRP'; its satellite records open here.
mc.i1: Raw: {m} MODIS + {v} VIIRS detections. Both satellites may have seen the same fire separately.
mc.i2: Separate clustering: MODIS forms one cluster, VIIRS another. Without merging the same fire would count as 2 events.
mc.i2one: This event has only {s}; there is no second satellite to merge.
mc.i3: Joint cluster: {n} detections form one event (no. {id}). Double counting avoided: 1 instead of 2.
mc.i3one: One event: {n} detections (no. {id}), from a single satellite.
mc.note: The outline is an approximate convex hull around the real points; MODIS squares are drawn axis-aligned.
btn.scimode_meas_tip: The MODIS-equivalent corrected series is only available without filters; the screen shows measured (uncorrected) counts. Reset filters, area, date range and sensor to default to return.
map.maxfire_t: Go to the event with the highest peak FRP (highest single detection, MW) among the filtered events
map.top_note: The default ranking is peak FRP (highest single detection in the event, MW): MODIS (1 km pixels) exists throughout 2000-2026, so peak FRP depends least on the number of satellites and old and new years compare more fairly. FRP is radiative power (MW), not energy or burned area.
map.top_note_sum: The FRP sum adds the instantaneous powers (MW) of all detections in the event; it is not energy or burned area. It grows with the number of satellites and overpasses (VIIRS after 2012, newer satellites from 2018 and 2023), so it is biased against older years.
frp.sum_note: FRP sum = sum of the detections' instantaneous radiative powers (MW) over overpasses; not energy or burned area.
map.top_single: {n} high-FRP events with a single detection are not listed: one pixel cannot be verified (may be a measurement artefact or a hot surface). They are still counted on the map and calendar.
raw.cut: (cap: first 400,000 points drawn; narrow the date range)
stg.nofire: Heat sources not counted as fires (shown on the map only)
stg.nofire.d: These are not part of event counts, the calendar or the cards. If you tick one, the map shows the raw detection points with that status in its own colour (+ marks); events do not change.
st.temiz.d: Counted as a fire: none of the reasons below applied. The label comes from our rules (NASA detection + cleaning rules).
st.aniz.d: Counted as a fire but shown separately: small, short, harvest-season events that look like field burning. The label is our rule (an estimate).
st.deniz.d: A hot spot at sea (oil platform, ship, flare). The label comes from NASA (type=3).
st.volkan.d: Heat of an active volcano. The label comes from NASA (type=1).
st.statik_nasa.d: A place NASA calls a 'static land source' (factory, refinery, mine and similar). The label comes from NASA (type=2).
st.sanayi.d: A facility NASA did not flag but that heats the same ~1 km cell for years in every season. The label comes from our industrial rule.
st.kalici_belirsiz.d: A source that recurs in the same cell unusually often but is not certainly a facility. The label comes from our rule (uncertain).
st.dusuk_guven.d: Low-confidence detection. No point has this status in this data version; low confidence is only a flag and does not change the status.
st.cnt_pt: {p} detection points — not counted as events, shown on the map in the raw-point layer
st.cnt_zero: 0 detection points — none in this data version
fx.aniz.label: Detect stubble with a per-province threshold
fx.aniz.help: The stubble threshold is taken from each province's own 'clean' detection median (never below the national threshold, never above 1.5x it); existing stubble events stay, only {n} extra events ({p}% of clean) become stubble. When on, numbers are computed in the browser instead of from the ready tables; when off, no number changes. Sanliurfa's clean share only moves {u0}% → {u1}%: the excess is not specific to Sanliurfa but an agricultural-plain effect (Adana, Diyarbakir, Konya and Mardin drop by a similar proportion). No documented large fire is affected; the moved events are small and short. The rule is an estimate (unverified).
fx.san.label: Exclude industrial-site residuals from counts
fx.san.help: Small, mostly single-pixel events ({s}, {ps}% of clean) that repeat for years in every season at factories and organised industrial zones (OpenStreetMap). None exceeds 100 MW or 10 detections; documented fires and their surroundings are protected. Default: these events are hidden on the map and in the top-FRP list but still counted in the numbers (cards, calendar, charts), so the scientific numbers do not change. Tick the box to remove them from the counts too; numbers are then computed in the browser. The rule is an estimate (unverified).
fx.san.show_d: Hidden on the map by default (counts do not change); when ticked they are drawn in the industrial colour as orange diamonds (◆).
fx.san.name: Industrial-site residuals (OSM, estimated)
fx.san.status_d: Small detections that recur for years at factory/OSB sites. By default still counted as clean events (scientific numbers do not change) but hidden on the map and in the top-FRP list. Change with the 'exclude industrial residuals from counts' box in the filter panel and the 'show' box on the map. The label comes from our rule (estimate).
fx.san.leg: Orange diamond: industrial-site residual (OSM industrial site, small detection recurring for years); estimate.
